newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban ban selected banknotes.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban ban selected banknotes.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban administration has banned 10,000-Afghani banknotes with a serial number of 33 or higher.
"All 10,000-Afghani banknotes with serial numbers starting with 33 or above are no longer valid." said Mawlavi Ihsanullah Ihsan, the head of the central bank in Kabul, on Tuesday.

The Taleban had previously banned the 10,000-Afghani notes that are in circulation in the northern areas outside Taleban control. These notes have several small but easily recognised printing variants.
The 10,000-Afghani note, which is worth about 50 cents, is Afghanistan's highest denomination banknote.
Mawlavi Ihsan said that other 10,000-Afghani notes in circulation are still valid.
Mawlavi Ihsan said the high series notes had been supplied to the ousted government of President Burbbani after the fall of Kabul to the Taleban on September 27.
The Taleban have yet to be recognised as the legitimate government of Afghanistan by any outside nation. The ousted government still occupies Afghanistan's seat in the United Nations.
The ousted government also still holds the contract with the printing company to print Afghanistan's currency.
The 32-series notes were the last to be processed through the central bank before the fall of Kabul.
Mawlavi Ihsan said the Taleban have no intention of reimbursing people holding the newly invalid notes.
The Taleban ban came after three days of speculation in Kabul's currency exchange.

Dealers on Sunday were already discounting the notes in anticipation of such a move. On Monday, the acting minister of finance in the Taleban administration told Reuters they had not banned the notes and did not intend to do so.
After 17 years of war, Afghanistan's industrial base has been shattered and the country has little or no reserves to back up the currency.
The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates that Afghanistan has seen 400 percent inflation since the beginning of the year.

Dealers in the exchange market say that the Taleban are trying to maintain the price of the Afghani, which rose when they took Kabul but has been steadily sliding ever since, by selling Pakistani rupees in the market.
